newsitem.title: FINLAND: YEAREND - Finland 1997 growth seen outpacing Europe.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Finland 1997 growth seen outpacing Europe.

text.p: Previously sceptical economists now believe Finland's economy will manage to grow faster than the rest of Europe in 1997, with slow inflation and a healthy current account surplus.
Most research institutes, banks and brokerages have recently upgraded forecasts in line with the finance ministry's projections, which a few months ago were seen as too optimistic.

The mean of eight 1997 Finnish GDP growth forecasts made in the past two months is 3.5 percent, with a range of between 2.5 and 4.6 percent. This year, Finnish GDP is seen rising 2.5 percent after 4.2 percent growth in 1995.
"In a European perspective, the pace of Finnish growth will be good," said Risto Murto, chief economist at brokerage Erik Selin Finance.
STRENGTH AT HOME AND ABROAD
Although slower than in Finland, growth elsewhere in Europe is expected to be sufficiently strong to keep Finnish exports on a sustained rising track, economists say.

Demand abroad for Finnish exports -- mainly paper, sawn timber, metal and engineering products, electrotechnical goods and chemicals -- combined with a strengthening boom in domestic consumption and a recovery in construction will fuel growth.
"Growth of up to four or five percent is not impossible," said Kirsi Hokka, economist at brokerage Alfred Berg.

"The export outlook is good, consumption prospects are good and it looks like construction is really taking off," she said, but added that her 3.5 percent growth forecast would stay unchanged at least until the first quarter of 1997.

Helped partly by a modest cut in 1997 income tax, private consumption is forecast to increase by between three and four percent. Real earnings will rise some 2.5 percent and consumer confidence is strong.
Ari Aaltonen, chief economist at bank Postipankki, sees "stable, accelerating and sustained growth".

The positive scenario, and growing confidence that Finland will be in the first wave of countries to join the single currency in 1999, should tighten the yield gap between Finnish bonds and benchmark German Bunds, economists say.
Aaltonen expects the 10-year spread to narrow to 10-15 basis points by the end of 1997 from 55 now. Murto at Erik Selin Finance sees it at between 20-40 basis points.
But Postipankki's forecast highlighted a key question dividing high and low 1997 GDP projections -- investment.
Forecasts for a rise in gross fixed capital formation range from just above two percent to 11 percent.
"To see strong growth in industrial investment we should already have heard of many corporate investment decisions. We haven't," Aaltonen said.
The industrial lobby warned late in November of a 16 percent fall in 1997 manufacturing industry investment versus the previous year.
Forecasting 2.1 percent 1997 investment growth, Aaltonen said three percent GDP growth in 1997 was the best Finland should expect.
"To reach five, or even four percent GDP growth would mean really stunning growth in private sector output," said.
"Because of the savings programmes still in effect, the public sector, which accounts for about one quarter of GDP, will grow by at most one percent next year," he added.
UNEMPLOYMENT STILL THE MAIN PROBLEM
Pellervo Economic Research Institute (PTT), ideologically close to the opposition Centre Party, said weak investment would keep 1997 GDP growth at around 2.5 percent.

Social Democrat Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen's government and the central bank were so intent on putting Finland in shape for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), that fiscal and monetary policies were too austere, PTT said.
"As a result, growth is too slow to reduce unemployment, our society's overwhelmingly most difficult problem," PTT said.
Unemployment is an increasingly sensitive issue for the left-right-green coalition, which in April 1995 set halving the jobless rate to between eight and nine percent by 1999 as its top priority.
While Finland is about to enter 1997 with long-term interest rates some three percentage points lower than two years ago, the jobless rate has barely budged.
In November, unemployment rose to 17.4 percent from 17.3 percent in October, according to labour ministry figures.

But economists across the board agree that Finnish inflation will remain low. Many welcomed central bank governor Sirkka Hamalainen's assessment on December 11 that conditions for slow inflation over the next few years remained "very favourable".

Forecasts for the year-on-year rise in 1997 CPI range from one to 1.8 percent. Consumer prices rose 0.7 percent in November while the partly EU-harmonised CPI gauge -- a refined version of which will be decisive for EMU -- rose by just 1.4 percent.
And most economists see the current account showing a surplus in excess of 20 billion markka ($4.33 billion) -- 3.5 percent of GDP -- next year. It was 15.4 billion markka in January-October.
